title: Data re-uploading in Quantum Machine Learning for time series: application to traffic forecasting
abstract_summary: This preprint applies quantum machine learning, specifically quantum variational circuits with data re-uploading, to short-term traffic flow forecasting using high-resolution loop detector data from Athens. The authors develop hybrid quantum-classical neural networks, compare them to classical deep learning models under a gap cross-validation protocol, and report that hybrid models with increased qubit counts and re-uploading blocks achieve competitive or improved accuracy, though at higher computational cost.
methodology_description: The study investigates hybrid quantum-classical neural network architectures for next-step traffic flow forecasting and compares them to purely classical baselines. Two experimental scenarios are considered: (A) replacing a classical fully-connected (FC) layer by a variational quantum layer (Quantum Variational Circuit, VQC) with a comparable information capacity, and (B) replacing an LSTM recurrence with a quantum data re-uploading layer that mimics recursive memory. Input windows of w=20 timesteps (traffic flow) are first compressed by a small LSTM-based autoencoder (encoder: one LSTM with 32 units + FC to Nq features). In Scenario A the encoder output (length Nq) feeds either a classical regressor whose first FC layer has 2*Nq neurons or a hybrid regressor whose first layer is a quantum layer acting on Nq qubits. In Scenario B the encoder output (sequence length Nq) feeds either an LSTM regressor with Nq units (recursing Nq times) or a quantum layer with Nq qubits and Nq data re-uploading blocks (each block = angle embedding of the input followed by parameterized rotations + entangling CNOTs). Quantum encoding uses angle/rotation embedding (Rx, Ry), entangling layers with trainable rotational gates and CNOTs, and Pauli-Z measurements to return classical values. Models are trained to minimize MSE using the Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.0005), minibatch size 32, up to 20 epochs. Evaluation uses 5-fold gap cross-validation (GapKFold) with a held-out validation set per fold; performance metrics reported are MSE, MAE and R2. Quantum circuits were simulated classically (PennyLane) with qubit counts varied (Nq in [2..14]), and the experiments examine convergence, predictive accuracy, and sensitivity to model complexity (number of qubits and number of re-uploading blocks).
experimental_setup: Classical simulation of hybrid quantum-classical models using PennyLane. Quantum layers were simulated on conventional hardware (no physical QPU); qubit counts were limited to Nq ≤ 14 due to classical simulation costs. Training used minibatches (32), Adam optimizer (lr=0.0005), up to 20 epochs, and 5-fold GapKFold cross-validation with gaps and a validation set per fold. Windowed time-series inputs of length 20 were preprocessed by an LSTM autoencoder to produce Nq-dimensional embeddings fed to either classical or quantum regressors.

experiment_input.source: Loop detector data from Syggrou Avenue (Athens, Greece) supplied via a Greek Government / Region of Attica database (academic access)
experiment_input.preprocessing: An LSTM-based autoencoder (encoder: LSTM with 32 units then FC to Nq features) used to compress input windows to Nq features. Train/validation/test splits created per fold using GapKFold with temporal gaps to avoid leakage.

experiment_process.overview: For each CV fold: generate windowed sequences after splicing train/val/test, train autoencoder (pre-training), encode each window to compressed embedding of length Nq, then train regressor (classical or hybrid) to predict next timestep.

scenarios.A: Fully connected scenario — encoder output (length Nq) fed to regressor. Classical regressor first layer: FC with 2*Nq neurons. Hybrid regressor first layer: quantum VQC acting on Nq qubits.
scenarios.B: Recursive scenario — encoder output (sequence length Nq) fed to recurrent regressor. Classical regressor: LSTM with Nq units (recursing Nq times). Hybrid regressor: quantum layer with Nq qubits and Nq data re-uploading blocks (each block = angle embedding + entangling layer).

experiment_process.quantum_circuit_design: Each re-upload block: angle embedding of classical inputs via single-qubit rotations (Rx,Ry), followed by a trainable entangling layer comprising parameterized single-qubit rotations (α,β,γ) and CNOT gates. Final measurement via Pauli-Z expectation per qubit to produce classical outputs.
experiment_process.evaluation: 5-fold GapKFold cross-validation with temporal gaps; a validation set precedes the test set in each fold; reported metrics computed on test folds.

experiment_output.predictions: Single scalar next-step traffic flow value per window
experiment_output.baselines: Classical equivalents (FC networks and LSTM regressors) matched in complexity under two equivalence schemes (information-size and recursion-count).
experiment_output.analysis_outputs: Training convergence plots (loss vs epochs), boxplots over CV folds for metrics, comparisons across qubit counts (Nq) and architectures, consistency checks vs fold ordering.

experiment_parameters.qubit_counts_tested: Nq in {2,4,6,8,10,12,14} (paper indicates range up to 14)
experiment_parameters.reupload_blocks: For Scenario B: number of re-upload blocks = Nq (one block per timestep of embedded sequence)
experiment_parameters.entangling_gates: CNOT plus parameterized single-qubit rotations (three parameters per rotation layer)

hardware_details: Quantum circuits were simulated classically using PennyLane (no physical QPU was used). Simulations were limited to small qubit counts (Nq ≤ 14) because of exponential classical simulation cost. No specific CPU/GPU or cloud provider details are reported in the manuscript.

key_findings: [supported] Hybrid quantum-classical neural networks (QNNs) applied to traffic forecasting can achieve predictive accuracy competitive with classical LSTM-based networks on the studied Athens loop-detector dataset.

[supported] Hybrid models that use data re-uploading (recursive quantum layers) outperform their classical counterparts in the recursive architecture (Scenario B) for configurations with approximately 6 qubits or more.

[supported] In fully connected architectures (Scenario A) where a classical FC layer is replaced by a quantum layer encoding comparable information, hybrid quantum layers underperform relative to classical FC layers (hybrid FC models converge slower and show inferior modeling power).
[supported] Increasing quantum-layer complexity (more qubits and more re-upload blocks) tends to improve hybrid model predictive accuracy in the experiments reported.

[supported] Simulations were limited by classical hardware: quantum-layer experiments were run with up to 14 qubits (Nq ≤ 14) and the authors report practical simulation scalability constraints for larger qubit counts.

[supported] Training quantum models (simulated QNNs) is more computationally expensive: the authors report that training a quantum model with Nq qubits took approximately two times longer per data re-upload block in their environment.

[supported] For the dataset and experimental setup used, all models typically converged within 20 epochs; many classical fully-connected models converged within ~3–4 epochs, while recursive/hybrid models flattened around ~5 epochs.
[supported] The study used a 5-fold gap cross-validation (GapKFold) protocol (with validation sets) to evaluate models and reports no significant bias from test-set positioning.
[speculative] The authors claim this is the first application of data re-uploading in a traffic prediction scenario (novelty claim relative to the transport forecasting literature).

[speculative] Data re-uploading can act analogously to a recurrent memory cell (e.g., LSTM-like behavior) because repeated re-encodings accumulate modifications to the quantum state and thereby capture temporal dependencies.

[speculative] Quantum Machine Learning (QML), and specifically data re-uploading approaches, hold promise for advancing traffic forecasting and could eventually offer advantages for ITS problems as quantum hardware improves.

[speculative] Increasing quantum model complexity on fault-tolerant or improved NISQ/post-NISQ hardware may yield tangible advantages over classical models in harder forecasting scenarios (larger/separate datasets, multi-input/multi-output).
[speculative] Data re-uploading variational circuits may help mitigate barren-plateau training issues (cited literature and discussed as a possible reason for trainability in these circuits).

[supported] Preprocessing with a small LSTM-based autoencoder (encoder only at inference) was used to capture temporal dependencies and reduce input dimensionality before the quantum/classical regressor comparison.
results_summary: The preprint reports a comparative study applying hybrid quantum-classical neural networks to a short-term traffic-volume forecasting task using 40 days of 1.5-minute-resolution data from a loop detector in Athens. Two scenarios were tested: (A) replacing a fully connected classical layer with a quantum layer of comparable encoded information and (B) replacing an LSTM-like recursive element with a quantum layer using data re-uploading. Empirical results (simulated with Pennylane) show hybrid recursive (data re-upload) architectures outperform classical LSTM equivalents for moderate qubit counts (≈6+ qubits) and that hybrid fully connected replacements underperform. Increasing the number of qubits and re-upload blocks improved hybrid performance, though simulations were limited to ≤14 qubits and incurred greater computational cost (roughly 2x slower per re-upload block). The authors present data re-uploading as a promising approach for time-series modeling but frame broader quantum advantage as contingent on improved hardware, noise mitigation, and further study.
performance_claims: Dataset: 40 days of traffic flow data at 1.5-minute resolution (~40 measurements/hour), yielding ~40,000 data points.
Window size for input sequences: w = 20 timesteps.
Evaluation protocol: 5-fold gap cross-validation (GapKFold) with validation sets; sequences generated post-splice to avoid leakage.
Quantum simulations limited to Nq ≤ 14 qubits due to classical simulation constraints.
In recursive architectures (Scenario B), hybrid QNNs outperform classical counterparts for Nq ≥ 6 qubits.
In fully connected architectures (Scenario A), classical and hybrid scores become comparable only from ~10 qubits onward; hybrid FC underperforms for smaller qubit counts.
Typical convergence: all models converged within 20 epochs; many classical FC models converged within ~3–4 epochs; recursive/hybrid models flattened around ~5 epochs.
Reported computational cost: training a quantum model with Nq qubits took approximately 2× longer per data re-uploading block in their simulation environment.
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors do not demonstrate a clear, general quantum advantage; they report competitive or superior results for hybrid recursive QNNs on a specific traffic dataset in classical simulation for modest qubit counts, but results are limited by classical simulation, small circuit sizes (≤14 qubits), and higher computational cost. The paper frames any practical quantum advantage as contingent on better quantum hardware, noise mitigation, and further validation on more challenging datasets.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Hybrid quantum-classical models with variational circuits and data re-uploading achieve competitive or improved forecasting accuracy (MSE/MAE/R2) vs matched classical baselines on short-term traffic time series.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Two hybrid scenarios studied: (A) replacing a classical FC layer with a VQC acting on compressed embeddings, and (B) replacing LSTM recurrence with a data re-uploading quantum layer to mimic recursion.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Experiments simulate VQCs with up to 14 qubits and show empirical trends in accuracy and convergence, indicating potential NISQ-era applicability for small time-series tasks, albeit with caveats.
#limitation:qubit-count — Classical simulation constrained experiments to Nq ≤ 14, limiting assessment of larger-qubit behaviour and scalability.
#limitation:simulation-only — All quantum layers were simulated on classical hardware (PennyLane); no experiments on physical QPUs were performed.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Claims of improved accuracy are based on classical simulation and cross-validation; no real-hardware validation to confirm robustness to noise or runtime costs on QPUs.

#limitation:data-encoding — The approach relies on angle/rotation encoding and an LSTM autoencoder to compress inputs to Nq features; encoding and preprocessing choices are central and may limit applicability or hide classical bottlenecks.
